primary_category.subcategory: A2.4 Information search, retrieval, gathering, and evaluation

evidence.quote: No forced entry, door was locked from inside, deadbolt engaged... We pulled her phone and found a breakup with her ex about three weeks prior, some heated texts.
evidence.explanation: The detective gathers and evaluates physical scene facts, digital records, and witness accounts to build an investigative picture.

evidence.quote: DNA didn't match him, and the coworker's second witness basically closed the two-hour gap we'd been counting on.
evidence.explanation: The detective receives and must evaluate new forensic and testimonial evidence against existing case facts, a core information-evaluation activity.

evidence.quote: the newest statement — the detailed one — got the most space and came across as the strongest piece in the file
evidence.explanation: Comparing and weighting witness statements for a referral memo is evidence evaluation and selection.

evidence.quote: Build a working theory fast enough to direct the canvass and get ahead of any warrant we'd need, but not so fast we lock ourselves in before the scene work comes back.
evidence.explanation: The detective plans a course of action under time pressure, weighing sequencing, resource allocation, and contingencies — non-routine problem resolution.

evidence.quote: We could've held off naming anybody until forensics and the full canvass were in, or we could've treated the rear-entrance sighting as equally weighted from the start.
evidence.explanation: Explicit generation and comparison of alternative courses of action toward an investigative goal.

evidence.quote: Experience, mostly. I've had cases where the ex is exactly who you think it is, and cases where it's a stranger.
evidence.explanation: The detective applies a generalized pattern derived from past cases to interpret the current facts, a form of abstraction beyond immediate case data.

evidence.quote: When I wrote the summary for the DA liaison, the newest statement — the detailed one — got the most space and came across as the strongest piece in the file
evidence.explanation: Drafting a written referral memo requires composing and structuring a narrative summary, a literacy task.

evidence.quote: My partner laid out the domestic-call history to the lieutenant and the rest of the group... nobody was formally tasked with running down the loitering lead.
evidence.explanation: The briefing involves allocating attention and (failing to) assign follow-up tasks among team members, a coordinating function, though the detective is not shown directly issuing the assignment.

not_observed_or_insufficient: A1.1 Strength - no evidence of physical exertion described
A1.2 Dexterity - no fine motor or instrument manipulation described
A1.3 Navigation - scene movement mentioned only in passing ('second-in on scene'), insufficient detail to classify
A2.1 Uncodified visual/auditory processing - scene observations are described but as discrete facts rather than pattern recognition of ambiguous perceptual signals
A2.3 Numeracy - only vague time estimates ('72 hours', 'two-hour gap') without calculation or quantitative reasoning
A3.1 Serving and attending - no direct assistance interaction with a victim, client, or member of the public is described
A3.2 Teaching, training, coaching - not evidenced
A3.3 Selling and influencing - the referral memo could imply persuasion of the DA liaison, but text does not show explicit persuasive framing, only descriptive weighting
ambiguities: A3.3 (Selling/influencing) versus A2.2 (Literacy) for the referral memo: the memo could be read as an attempt to persuade the DA liaison toward one suspect, but the transcript frames it as writing/summarizing rather than deliberate advocacy, so it was excluded as a secondary category rather than included with low confidence.

A2.1 versus A2.4 for the initial scene assessment: interpreting the locked door and contained scene could be classified as uncodified perceptual pattern recognition, but the transcript presents it as an evaluated fact set rather than a raw perceptual judgment, so it was placed under A2.4.

evidence.quote: I chose to name him primary and put resources there
evidence.explanation: The detective personally decides resource allocation and suspect prioritization, indicating meaningful discretion, though the decision is later shaped and formalized by group and supervisory context.

evidence.quote: the lieutenant didn't push back, so we had a direction the whole unit could move on together
evidence.explanation: A lieutenant is present and could have intervened or redirected the investigation, indicating supervisory oversight, though the oversight is passive rather than an active audit or approval gate in this episode.

evidence.quote: The DA liaison ended up asking for supplemental work before filing on either of them.
evidence.explanation: The DA liaison functions as an external reviewing authority whose approval is required before charges can proceed, indicating a formal review checkpoint.

evidence.quote: My partner and I caught it together — we split the canvass and the paperwork most of the time.
evidence.explanation: The detective works with a partner and shares case tasks directly.

evidence.quote: My partner laid out the domestic-call history to the lieutenant and the rest of the group
evidence.explanation: Decisions are shaped by a group briefing involving the partner, lieutenant, and junior detectives, showing collaborative joint decision-making.

evidence.quote: Every step had something behind it. It's only looking at it end to end now that I can see where things could've gone differently.
evidence.explanation: The case is presented as a singular, evolving sequence of non-repeating decisions rather than recurring identical actions.

evidence.quote: We had the usual clock — 72 hours or so before witness memory gets soft
evidence.explanation: Reference to a customary investigative timeframe suggests an implicit procedural norm, though no explicit checklist or script is described.

evidence.quote: drafting the referral for the DA liaison
evidence.explanation: Preparing a referral memo for a DA liaison implies a standardized organizational handoff procedure.

evidence.quote: DNA didn't match him, and the coworker's second witness basically closed the two-hour gap we'd been counting on.
evidence.explanation: Key evidentiary inputs shift unpredictably across the case, indicating low certainty of conditions and outcomes.

evidence.quote: That was a harder morning. DNA didn't match him... rather than shift the whole frame onto him immediately, I treated the DNA gap as something forensics might still explain
evidence.explanation: The detective must respond to unexpected disconfirming evidence that disrupts the established theory, requiring real-time reassessment.

tools.role_in_task: Reviewing digital phone records and communications as case evidence

evidence.quote: We pulled her phone and found a breakup with her ex about three weeks prior, some heated texts.
evidence.explanation: Extracting and reviewing phone data is a basic digital information-retrieval activity, though the specific extraction tool/software is not named.

tools.role_in_task: Case log and lab/DNA result tracking system

evidence.quote: Swabs go to the lab... the case log had the ex documented as primary suspect
evidence.explanation: References to a maintained case log and forensic lab processing imply use of specialized law-enforcement case-management and forensic-tracking systems, though the interview does not describe direct hands-on system use by the participant.

task_anchors.task_description: Assessing physical scene conditions (locked door, contained scene) and pulling victim's phone records to form an initial evidentiary picture.
Naming the ex-partner as primary suspect and allocating investigative resources based on weighted circumstantial evidence.
Unit briefing where the team collectively formalizes the primary-suspect theory and does not assign follow-up to a dissenting lead.
Reassessing case theory upon receipt of a negative DNA result and a closed alibi gap.
Drafting a written referral memo for the DA liaison, weighting and presenting witness statements of differing recency and detail.

evidence: I chose to name him primary and put resources there — the domestic call history plus the locked door plus the breakup timing
My partner laid out the domestic-call history to the lieutenant and the rest of the group... nobody was formally tasked with running down the loitering lead
DNA didn't match him, and the coworker's second witness basically closed the two-hour gap we'd been counting on
When I wrote the summary for the DA liaison, the newest statement — the detailed one — got the most space

missing_evidence: No description of specific software, databases, or ICT systems used to review phone records, DNA lab results, or the case log, limiting tool-category precision.
No description of physical scene-walking, canvassing legwork, or navigation detail beyond high-level summary, limiting assessment of A1.3.
No detail on how the DA liaison responded beyond requesting supplemental work, limiting assessment of A3.3 (selling/influencing).
